Am Dienstag begann die Rückgabe der Schulgeräte in der kleinen Ausgabestelle neben der Bibliothek. Die Geräte sollten nicht einfach auf den Tisch gelegt werden, weil die Nummern auf den Gehäusen erst mit der Liste im RowanSync abgeglichen werden mussten. Ich war ab halb acht dort und habe zuerst die grauen Kisten aus dem Lager geholt. Frau Kern hatte am Vortag gesagt, dass die Rückgabe bis zwölf dauern könnte, falls die Klassen ihre Sachen nicht gesammelt bringen. Um acht kamen die ersten beiden Schüler aus der 7b mit einem Tablet, einem Ladegerät und einer Schutztasche. Sie hatten alles in eine Stofftasche gepackt und wussten nicht mehr, welches Ladegerät zu welchem Tablet gehörte.

Ich erklärte ihnen, dass wir die Seriennummern einzeln prüfen und danach die Sachen in die passende Kiste legen. Sie fragten, ob sie gleich gehen könnten. „Ja“, sagte ich, „nachdem ich den Zustand und die Zubehörteile notiert habe, könnt ihr gehen.“ Das Ja war eine direkte Antwort und keine Pause. Ich habe die Schüler gebeten, bei einem fehlenden Teil den Namen der Klasse auf den Zettel zu schreiben und nicht zu raten. Sie warteten, während ich die Etiketten verglich. Bei einem Tablet war die obere Ecke der Hülle eingerissen. Das Gerät selbst hatte aber keinen sichtbaren Schaden. Ich schrieb beides getrennt auf, damit später niemand die Hülle mit dem Tablet verwechselt.

Um Viertel nach acht kam Herr Beck aus dem Naturwissenschaftsraum mit einem Laptopwagen und sagte, dass ein Rad beim Schieben blockiere. Er bat mich, den Wagen trotzdem mitzunehmen, weil er im Gang stehe. Ich sagte, dass ich zuerst die Rückgabe der Laptops aufnehmen müsse und danach den Wagen ansehen könne. Er antwortete: „Das ist in Ordnung, ich stelle ihn an die Markierung neben dem Fenster.“ Dort war genug Platz und der Fluchtweg blieb frei. In der Zwischenzeit öffnete ich die Liste für die 8a im RowanSync und stellte fest, dass dort zwölf Tablets eingetragen waren, aber nur elf auf dem Wagen lagen. Ich prüfte die Fächer noch einmal und fand ein Tablet unter einem zusammengefalteten Tuch.

1. Ich habe die Gerätenummer auf dem Tablet mit der Nummer in der Liste verglichen.
2. Ich habe den Bildschirm und die Kanten auf sichtbare Schäden geprüft.
3. Ich habe Ladegerät und Hülle als eigenes Zubehör erfasst.
4. Ich habe den Namen der rückgebenden Klasse und die Uhrzeit eingetragen.

Bei einem Gerät fehlte das Ladegerät. Der Schüler sagte: „Ich glaube, es ist noch im Raum, aber ich kann es gerade nicht bestätigen.“ Ich schrieb „fehlend, noch nicht bestätigt“ und ließ das Feld für die spätere Nachtragung offen. Das ist wichtig, weil ein nicht bestätigtes Teil nicht als endgültig verloren gelten soll. Auf dem Ablagebrett lagen außerdem zwei Ladegeräte ohne Nummer. Ich legte sie nicht zu einer Klasse, sondern in die kleine Fundkiste.

Gegen neun kam Frau Kern dazu und fragte, ob die Geräte aus dem Musikraum schon zurück seien. Ich sagte, dass eine Kiste mit vier Tablets angekommen sei, aber dass ich die Etiketten noch nicht vollständig prüfen konnte. Sie sah auf die Uhr und sagte: „Dann schreib bitte nicht schon erledigt, bevor die letzte Nummer stimmt.“ Ich ließ den Status offen und setzte einen kurzen Vermerk für die Musiklehrerin daneben. Sie hatte am Morgen angerufen und gebeten, die Kiste getrennt zu halten, weil ein Tablet für eine Prüfung am Nachmittag gebraucht werden könnte. Ich stellte die Kiste auf das obere Fach und klebte den Zettel außen auf die Seite, damit er beim Stapeln nicht verdeckt wird.

Um zehn vor zehn brachte die 6c ihre Geräte in einem Rollkorb. Die Klassenlehrerin zählte vor Ort sieben Tablets und drei Kopfhörer. Die Liste nannte sieben Tablets und vier Kopfhörer. Sie schaute in den Korb und sagte: „Einer liegt vielleicht noch im Vorbereitungsraum.“ Ich nahm diese Aussage als Möglichkeit auf und änderte die Anzahl nicht, solange niemand das Teil gefunden hatte. Ein Tablet ließ sich nicht einschalten. Ich steckte es nicht selbst an ein anderes Ladegerät, weil dessen Zuordnung unklar war. Stattdessen notierte ich, dass der Bildschirm dunkel blieb, und bat die Lehrerin, den Namen des Schülers zu ergänzen, der das Gerät zuletzt benutzt hatte. Sie wollte die Information bis zum Ende des Tages nachreichen.

Als Herr Beck später zurückkam, habe ich das blockierte Rad am Laptopwagen vorsichtig geprüft. Es drehte sich nicht frei, und an der Achse lag ein kurzes Stück Schnur. Ich entfernte es nicht, weil der Wagen noch beladen war und eine Kiste hätte abrutschen können. Ich sagte Herrn Beck, dass der Wagen erst entladen werden müsse, bevor ich weiter nachsehe. Er meinte: „Ich räume die Laptops nach meiner Stunde aus und melde mich dann.“ Ich ließ den Wagen an der Markierung stehen und notierte den Zustand auf einem separaten Zettel. Diese Reparatur war kein Teil der Geräterückgabe, aber der Wagen gehörte ebenfalls zur Ausstattung der Schule und sollte deshalb nicht ohne Hinweis im Gang bleiben.

Kurz vor elf prüfte ich die offenen Einträge mit Frau Kern. Bei dem fehlenden Ladegerät aus der 7b gab es noch keine Bestätigung, und die 6c hatte den vierten Kopfhörer weiterhin nicht gefunden. Wir ließen beide Angaben offen. Frau Kern bat mich, die Listen nicht zu schließen, falls die Rückmeldungen vor zwölf einträfen. Sie sagte, dass sie die Nachträge selbst gegenzeichnen könne, sobald sie die Geräte oder eine klare Rückmeldung gesehen habe. Ich legte die offenen Zettel oben auf den Ordner und nicht in die abgeschlossene Kiste. Zwei Klassen hatten die Rückgabe bereits vollständig bestätigt, und ihre Kisten waren mit Datum und Raumnummer beschriftet.

Um halb zwölf brachte ein Schüler aus der 7b tatsächlich ein Ladegerät zurück. Er sagte: „Das lag noch unter dem Tisch, ich habe es eben gefunden.“ Ich verglich die Anschlussform und die kleine Nummer auf dem Etikett mit dem Tablet aus seinem ersten Besuch und trug die Rückgabe ein. Der vierte Kopfhörer der 6c war zu diesem Zeitpunkt noch nicht da. Frau Kern musste zu einer Besprechung und sagte, sie komme nach der Mittagspause wieder auf die offenen Zettel zurück. Ich ließ den Eintrag deshalb offen und stellte die Kopfhörerzählung nicht auf vollständig.

Am Ende der Vormittagsschicht brachte ich die Kisten in den verschlossenen Geräteraum. Die Musikraumkiste blieb oben im Regal, getrennt von den anderen, und der Wagen von Herrn Beck blieb an der Markierung, weil er noch nicht entladen war. Auf dem Tisch lagen nur die zwei nummernlosen Ladegeräte und die offenen Zettel für die 6c sowie für den Laptopwagen. Ich schrieb die Uhrzeit des letzten Prüfschritts auf das Deckblatt und gab Frau Kern den Ordner persönlich zurück. Falls der vierte Kopfhörer gefunden wird, muss die Klassenliste vor dem Schließen ergänzt werden. Falls er nicht auftaucht, bleibt die bisherige Zählung als offene Differenz stehen.

On Thursday, May 18, I met the delivery at the North Quay market just before seven in the morning. The stall is on the east side of the covered arcade beside the blue post, not the entrance facing the bus stop. I got there at 6:40 because the driver had asked us to leave room for his hand trolley between the flower stand and our table. The forecast said showers after lunch, and the pavement was already damp, but there was no rain while we unloaded. Mara, our stall lead, had the key to the padlock, and I had the paper order and a pencil. The driver was Leon from Bell Orchard, and he said the van had left the farm at 5:20 after the cold-room check.

We received fourteen wooden crates of strawberries, six shallow trays of rhubarb, two sacks of spinach, and a small box of mint. The strawberry crates were marked with the picking date, and the rhubarb trays had blue tape around the corners. One crate had a split slat, but the fruit inside looked intact. I counted the crates twice because the first count came to thirteen—no, fourteen—and Mara counted them again with me. The invoice listed the same quantities except it called the mint a mixed herb box. Leon said that was how their printer described it, and I wrote “mint” on our stall copy. The order total was two hundred and eighty-six pounds, including the twelve-pound delivery fee, which we had agreed by email on Monday.

While we were checking the fruit, Mara asked whether the strawberries had stayed in the chilled part of the van. Leon said yes; the temperature display had read four degrees when they left and five degrees when he opened the back doors here at the arcade. I asked if the display reading was written on his sheet. He said, “It is on the route copy in the cab.” He went back to get it, and the route copy showed four degrees at departure and five degrees at arrival. It did not show a reading for the drive itself. Mara said, “Right, that answers the question for the arrival time,” and then she wrote both numbers on the receiving sheet. She did not say that we had checked the temperature throughout the trip.

1. Mara checked the strawberries for soft patches and set the split crate on the lower shelf so it would not be lifted again.

3. We checked the spinach sacks and found one damp patch on the outside, but the leaves in that sack were dry.
4. I put the mint box in the lidded tub away from the strawberries because the mint smell was strong enough to carry across the table.
5. Leon took away the empty hand trolley and left the wooden crates stacked behind the stall.

At 7:10, we put the price cards out but did not start selling the strawberries until Mara had taken a photograph of the split crate and the short rhubarb tray. She sent the pictures to our shared account and wrote that the strawberry fruit appeared intact and that one rhubarb tray seemed underweight. Leon said, “Send me the photo too, and I will attach it to the route record.” I sent it to the number on his delivery slip. He replied that he had received it and would pass it to the orchard office. He did not offer a replacement or say that the invoice would change, and we did not ask him to decide either point at the stall.

The remaining strawberries stayed in the shaded front display, and we kept the damp spinach sack separate so its outer surface would not touch the other produce. I asked Mara whether she wanted me to update the shared account with that information, and she said not yet because the delivery photos and the weather note were enough for now. She asked me to keep the paper order beside the receiving sheet until she had compared the invoice with the orchard reply.

When I left at 2:30, the short rhubarb tray was still listed as a question on the receiving sheet, and the invoice total remained two hundred and eighty-six pounds. The orchard office had not replied yet. Mara had the delivery slip and the route copy, and I put the stall copy in the blue folder in the drawer. Wir haben im Team am Montag die Migration unserer Dokumente aus dem alten Laufwerk in den neuen gemeinsamen Speicher besprochen. Diese Bedingung gilt auch dann, wenn die Abweichung nur aus temporären Dateien besteht, weil wir erst sicher wissen müssen, welche Dateien dazugehören. Falls eine Abweichung größer ist, verschieben wir diesen Termin und informieren die drei Abteilungen bis zwölf Uhr über den neuen Stand. Wenn alles innerhalb der vereinbarten Grenze liegt, beginnt Jonas um acht Uhr mit dem Kopieren, und Mara bleibt bis zehn Uhr für Rückfragen erreichbar. Die Mitarbeiter sollen am Dienstag bis zum Ende der Umstellung keine neuen Dateien in den alten Ordnern anlegen. Neue Dokumente kommen in den gemeinsamen Speicher, und vorhandene Dokumente können sie dort erst nach der Freigabe durch ihre Fachabteilung bearbeiten.

Am Mittwoch wollen wir die offenen Punkte gemeinsam ansehen und entscheiden, welche davon noch eine fachliche Antwort brauchen. Die alte Version bleibt bis zum Ende der zwei Monate lesbar, damit niemand für eine frühere Datei auf eine private Kopie zurückgreifen muss. Danach soll die Teamleitung den Archivzugriff erneut prüfen. Sie hat noch nicht zugesagt, dass der alte Speicher anschließend gelöscht wird, und wir haben das auch nicht als Beschluss notiert. Bis dahin sammelt Mara die ausgefüllten Prüfblätter, Jonas bewahrt das technische Protokoll im Migrationsordner auf, und ich halte die Liste der offenen Fragen aktuell. Wenn eine Abteilung vor dem Mittwoch einen Fehler meldet, nehme ich ihn in diese Liste auf und vermerke, wer ihn prüfen soll. Der nächste Schritt für uns ist damit klar: die Testläufe durchführen, die tatsächlichen Zählungen vergleichen und erst danach anhand der vereinbarten Bedingung über den Termin der vollständigen Umstellung sprechen.

We are setting up the desktop uploader for the West Annex archive, and this is the first week of the pilot, not a production migration. The team has six staff accounts and two shared workstations: one at the intake desk and one in the scanning room. The uploader will send completed batches to the archive team's staging folder on the internal server. The folder is called West Annex Intake, and the server address is already saved in the app. The request is to configure the desktop client, not to change permissions on the server or reorganize the existing folders. The archive coordinator said, “We need the upload screen to be simple enough for a volunteer to use without guessing.”

We will test on a Windows workstation named WA Scan 02 and a Mac workstation named WA Intake 01. Both are connected to the office network, but the Mac sometimes sleeps during lunch. The Windows machine stays logged in at the intake desk until the last shift leaves. We have a 250-megabyte file limit for each scan batch and a daily target of 18 batches. The limit is per batch, not per individual image. A batch usually contains between 12 and 35 images. The scans are mostly PDF files, with a few JPEG receipts, and the current naming pattern starts with the date, then the collection code, then a four-digit sequence. The sample name is 2025-04-16-MAP-0038.pdf. Please keep that sample unchanged in the setup notes because staff use it when checking filenames.

For the upload settings, we want the client to check for new files every 10 minutes and show a visible notification when a batch completes. The notification should include the destination folder and the batch name, but not the full server address. We do not want a sound alert because the scanning room is also used for interviews. The progress display should show transferred size as well as percentage, and it should keep the last five completed batches in the local history. The history is for troubleshooting only and should not become a second copy of the scans. The local cache can retain unfinished transfers for up to 48 hours; then staff will review and clear them on Monday morning. If the network is unavailable, the client should wait rather than repeatedly opening a connection.

There is one setting whose exact key needs to go into the configuration request on its own line:
transfer.allow_resume
Please enable that setting so a transfer interrupted by a short network drop can continue from the point it stopped rather than starting over. The setting applies to uploads only and does not change how files are edited or saved locally. We have not yet tested a complete interruption and recovery, so the setup note should describe the intended behavior without saying that the test has passed. The coordinator asked whether resuming would create duplicate files, and the answer is not known for this client yet. Please leave that question open for the vendor instead of treating it as resolved.

We need a retry policy for ordinary connection failures. The client should make three retries with a pause of 30 seconds between attempts. If all three retries fail, it should leave the batch in the queue and show a warning for the next staff member. The retry count refers to attempts after the first upload attempt, so there can be four attempts in total. Do not delete or rename a queued file after a failure. A staff member may move it manually once the network issue is understood. If a file exceeds the 250-megabyte batch limit, the uploader should display a separate limit warning and leave the batch untouched. This limit warning is not the same as the connection warning and should not trigger retries.

1. Account and access: Use the shared uploader account already created by the archive administrator. Do not save its password in a printed checklist. The two workstations should use the same destination and settings but retain separate local histories.

2. Schedule and status: Keep automatic checks at 10-minute intervals and show a completion notification only after every file in that batch has arrived in staging. If one file is still transferring, the batch is not complete.

3. File handling: Preserve the original filenames and do not compress the scans during upload. The archive staff will perform any renaming or format conversion after the files have been received.

4. Recovery test: Run one normal upload on each workstation, then briefly disconnect the network during a small test batch and observe whether the client resumes. If it does not resume, record what happened and contact the vendor. Do not run this interruption test with a live collection.

Friday afternoon is the first review time with the coordinator, and the vendor representative may join by video if available. Greenhouse watering rota

The rota covers the east and west houses at Bellmere Community Greenhouse, where six volunteers share the morning watering work from Monday through Saturday. The doors open at 7:30, and the first person on duty signs the clipboard beside the potting bench before turning on any valves. Sunday is reserved for inspection rather than routine watering. The rota is posted on the noticeboard by the entrance and copied into the shared calendar, so a volunteer can check the week without relying on a message from the previous person.

Each shift usually takes between forty and fifty minutes. The east house contains the seedling tables, the herb bench, and the row of young citrus trees; the west house holds tomatoes, peppers, and the larger pots of overwintered plants. The labels on the benches use the same letters as the watering map. Volunteers carry a blue can for seedlings and a green can for pots that are not connected to the drip line. The two cans have different rose heads, and both are stored upside down to keep dust out.

The first volunteer checks the rain gauge and the moisture meter before deciding which zones need water. The meter is useful, but it does not replace a look at the compost: a dry surface can cover damp soil below, especially after a cool night. The seedling trays are checked at the corners as well as in the middle because the outer cells dry first. If the leaves are already wet from condensation, the volunteer waters the compost carefully rather than spraying the foliage. A short note on the clipboard records which zones were watered and which were left for another check.

The rota has a few practical rules that prevent one shift from undoing the work of another. Water is applied slowly, with a pause between passes, so it can soak into the pots instead of running across the bench. The drip line is turned on only after the filter has been checked for grit, and it is turned off at the tap rather than by pulling the tubing. Seedlings get small amounts more often; established citrus trees get a deeper soak when the soil is dry several centimetres down. No one adds feed during a watering shift, since feed days are marked separately on the calendar.

1. Monday: Nia checks the seedling trays in the east house and waters the herb bench if the compost is dry below the surface. She also empties the rain gauge and writes the reading on the clipboard.
2. Tuesday: Omar inspects the west-house drip line, cleans its filter if needed, and waters the tomato and pepper pots that are not receiving enough from the line.
3. Wednesday: Lena covers both houses, with extra attention to the young citrus trees. She notes any leaves with curled edges and leaves the pots alone if their lower compost is still damp.
4. Thursday: Peter checks the seedling corners and the larger west-house pots. He compares the moisture meter reading with the compost before choosing whether to use the blue or green can.
5. Friday and Saturday: Mei and Rowan take one day each, in that order. They check the previous notes, water only the zones that need it, and leave a clear entry for whoever comes next.

The schedule changes when someone is away, but swaps are written on the clipboard and entered in the shared calendar before the shift starts. A volunteer who cannot make a morning should contact the next person on the list and agree on a replacement, rather than assuming that the next person will arrive early. Last month, Nia traded her Tuesday for Rowan’s Thursday because of a class, and both dates were changed in the calendar. “I can cover the west house, but I can’t take the whole morning,” Omar said when another swap was proposed, so Lena agreed to handle the east house that day.

A low reading in the cistern changes the order of work. If the water level is below the painted yellow mark, volunteers water the seedling trays and the newly planted citrus first, then check the west-house pots and leave any that remain damp. They do not use the reserve barrel unless the coordinator has confirmed that the cistern valve is working properly. This condition matters most in hot weather, when the cistern can fall quickly and the reserve barrel is also needed for the public planting beds. The person who finds the level below the mark writes the reading and the time beside the day’s entry.

On Saturday afternoon, the coordinator reviews the notes and checks for patterns rather than judging a shift by the amount of water used. A tray that dries out twice in one week may need to be moved away from the warm glass, while a wet corner beneath the west-house bench may point to a leaking joint. Volunteers are asked to report a leak promptly and to put a small tray beneath a slow drip until it can be repaired. The greenhouse keeps spare washers, a filter brush, and two hose connectors in the labelled drawer under the potting bench; tools go back there after use.

The rota is intended to make care predictable without making volunteers follow it blindly. Weather, plant size, and the condition of the compost can change what a particular shift needs to do, so the written notes explain decisions as well as actions. When a zone is deliberately left dry, the volunteer records that choice and the reason, such as damp lower soil or a recent rain. If the cistern is below the yellow mark, the seedling and newly planted citrus priorities still apply even when the usual shift holder is away. At the end of each shift, the tap is closed, the cans are returned to their hooks, and the clipboard is left open to the next blank line.

I am forwarding the dye log for the north room run from Tuesday through Thursday because the mill office asked for the pages before its Friday review. The log covers the slate blue wool lot and the two smaller cotton lots that shared the rinse line this week. The wool came from bale group W seventeen, and the cotton came from bins C four and C six. The cover sheet says the room opened at six ten on Tuesday, and the first dye bath reached its target temperature at seven twenty-eight. The operator on that shift was Lenora Price, and the second reader was Miguel Santos.

The slate blue recipe was entered at the west bench using the card dated May twelve. The target shade was listed as harbor slate, and the bath called for six kilograms of dye powder, seventy-four liters of water, and four hundred grams of salt. The log gives a starting pH of six point two and a final pH of five point eight. The bath was held at eighty-six degrees for forty minutes before the first swatch was removed. The wool lot was weighed at twelve point four kilograms before it went into the kettle, and the empty basket weight was recorded separately so the net figure could be checked.

There is a note beside the first swatch that says the left edge looked slightly warmer under the inspection lamp. The second swatch was judged closer to the card and was pinned to the board with its time marked as eight oh five. The operator wrote that the room lamp had been replaced on Monday and that the new bulb made the navy samples look brighter than they did at the window. The shade was not changed in response. The log keeps the original recipe and identifies the second swatch as the reference for this run. The sample envelope is in the clear drawer under the west bench.

The cotton lots used a separate bath after the wool kettle had been rinsed. The first cotton bin was C four, and the second was C six. Each was weighed on the floor scale before loading, and each scale reading was copied into the log by Miguel. The water meter showed one hundred twelve liters for the combined cotton bath, and the salt came from the sealed blue pail near the steam valve. The note records a brief pause when the mixer belt slipped at ten sixteen. The belt was reset, and the bath resumed at ten twenty-one with no additional dye powder entered on the page.

The numbered checks on the final page are grouped under Rinse and Finish:
1. Rinse water was clear at the outlet after the third change, and the outlet temperature was thirty-one degrees.
2. Both cotton lots were checked for loose color with a white cloth, and no transfer was recorded.
3. The slate blue wool swatch was dried on the upper rack rather than the lower rack because the lower rail was damp.
4. The finished wool weight was eleven point eight kilograms, and the combined cotton weight was eight point six kilograms. The scale ticket is clipped behind this section.

A yellow note from the morning shift says, “Please leave the sample envelope closed until the office has compared the swatches with the card.” The note is initialed by R. P. and dated Wednesday morning. The office comparison has not been entered in this log. The envelope remains in the clear drawer, and the board still displays the second swatch. The log also says that if the office requests another sample, the operator should cut it from the end of the wool piece and not from the shoulder where the weave is tighter. That condition matters because the remaining piece is reserved for the order check.

The room temperature entries were recorded at the start and end of each shift. Tuesday began at eighteen degrees and ended at twenty-one. Wednesday began at nineteen and ended at twenty. Thursday began at seventeen and ended at nineteen. The exhaust fan reading stayed between four hundred ten and four hundred twenty cubic meters per hour. The maintenance card on the wall lists a filter change for the previous Friday and no further service during the dye run. The entries are in the narrow column at the far right and are easy to miss when the log is folded.

There are two marks beside the rinse line that need to remain visible. One is a blue pencil circle around the ten sixteen belt note, and the other is a small check beside the final outlet temperature. The page was copied from the bound room book on Thursday afternoon, and the original is stored in cabinet B under the yearly dye records. The copy has a faint gray line through the lower margin, but none of the quantities are covered. The ticket behind the final page carries the scale serial number eight two one six and a calibration date of April third.

The mill office asked that the forwarded pages include the cover sheet, the recipe page, the numbered rinse and finish checks, and the scale ticket. I am forwarding those pages together in that order. The sample envelope is not among them, and the office comparison is still absent from the log. The condition about cutting any requested sample from the end of the wool piece is written beside the envelope note, so it remains with the record if the office asks for one later. The final page has a blank space for the comparison date, and that space is still blank.
